```{r opts, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

PlotTrellis turns your sequencing data into multi-track genomic figures (transcript counts,
transcript structures, splice junctions, coverage, comparisons between samples), in a
point-and-click app or in a few lines of R.

# Installation

PlotTrellis is not on CRAN, so `repos` tells R where to find it and its Bioconductor
dependencies (from scratch this can take up to 15 minutes):

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("PlotTrellis", repos = c("https://aleks-wehi.r-universe.dev",
                                          "https://bioc.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
```

# Your first figure in the app

PlotTrellis ships one example: mouse mammary basal cells (Basal) and luminal progenitors (LP)
around the *Elf5*, *Ehf* and *Cat* genes.

```{r app-example, eval=FALSE}
BiocManager::install("org.Mm.eg.db")   # mouse gene annotation (for human data: "org.Hs.eg.db")
library(PlotTrellis)
run_plottrellis(project_dir = "PlotTrellis-example", samples_txt = pt_example())
```

`project_dir` is the folder that holds everything PlotTrellis makes for this project. Here it
is created in R's working directory, but it can be any folder. `pt_example()` gives
the path of the example's `samples.txt`.

The app opens with *Elf5* and its tracks already picked: click **Generate figure**. Then try
*Ehf* or *Cat*, or a different set of tracks.

To build your own figure on the **Compose** page, choose how many samples and which ones, then
a gene or coordinates:

```{r compose-screenshot-1, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/sample_and_gene_selection.png")
```

Drag tracks into the figure (drag again to reorder) and click **Generate figure**. The title,
fonts, heights and colours are under **Figure settings**. The **Output** page downloads the
figure as an SVG or as a standalone R script, and shows the gene's transcripts and protein
domains.

```{r compose-screenshot-2, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/track_composer.png")
```

To use PlotTrellis from R code instead, see
[Your first figure in code](#your-first-figure-in-code) below.

# Your own data

The simplest way is to run the command above with a new `project_dir` and no `samples_txt`:

```{r own-data, eval=FALSE}
run_plottrellis(project_dir = "my-project")
```

A wizard guides you through listing your samples and their files, and saves them in the
project folder. When you click **Save** (or **Close**), close that browser tab: the app
reopens in a new tab from RStudio a few seconds later.

```{r wizard-screenshot, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/wizard_manual.png")
```

Apart from your data, the one file you need is your genome's **GTF**: the annotation file
that says where each gene and transcript is. Use the one your data was aligned or quantified
with, if you have it. Otherwise download it from [GENCODE](https://www.gencodegenes.org)
(human and mouse: the "Comprehensive gene annotation" GTF) or
[Ensembl](https://www.ensembl.org/info/data/ftp/) (other species), for the same genome
build as your data. It can stay gzipped (`.gtf.gz`).

# Your first figure in code

The rest of this vignette is for working in R. The example figure from the app:

```{r code-example, eval=FALSE}
library(PlotTrellis)
proj <- pt_project(project_dir = "PlotTrellis-example", samples_txt = pt_example())
fig  <- pt_figure(proj, "Elf5", tracks = c("atac@Basal", "atac@LP",
                                           "transcript_counts@Basal", "transcript_counts@LP",
                                           "transcripts_annotated", "genes"))
pt_save(fig, "Elf5.pdf")   # or .svg, .png
```

```{r code-example-run, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="Elf5 in mouse mammary basal cells and luminal progenitors: ATAC coverage and transcript counts for each, then the annotated transcripts and the gene."}
library(PlotTrellis)
proj <- pt_project(project_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "PlotTrellis-example"), samples_txt = pt_example())
pt_figure(proj, "Elf5", tracks = c("atac@Basal", "atac@LP",
                                   "transcript_counts@Basal", "transcript_counts@LP",
                                   "transcripts_annotated", "genes"))
```

# Your own data in code (writing a samples.txt)

A project can also come from a `samples.txt`, a tab-separated table with one row per
sample under a few header lines. For example:

```
# data_root: /data/smithlab/tcell_2026
# gtf_path: /data/reference/gencode.v44.annotation.gtf.gz
# orgdb: org.Hs.eg.db
# genome_label: hg38
condition  colour   bw:atac                 paired-end:junctions        quantdir:salmon
Control    #1b9e77  atac/Control_merged.bw  junctions/Control_SJ.bed    salmon/Control
KO         #d95f02  atac/KO_merged.bw       junctions/KO_SJ.bed         salmon/KO
```

The header lines:

- `data_root`: the folder your data files are in. The paths in the table are relative to it.
- `gtf_path`: your genome's GTF file (see above).
- `orgdb`: your species' annotation package, e.g. `org.Mm.eg.db` (mouse), `org.Hs.eg.db` (human).
- `genome_label`: the genome build's UCSC name, e.g. `mm10`, `hg38`.

The columns (separated by tabs):

- `condition`: the sample's name.
- `colour` (optional): the sample's colour.
- One column per kind of data file, headed `type:name`. The type says what the file is, and the
  name is what you call the track: `bw:atac` holds bigWig files and gives tracks called `atac`.

| Type | File | Track |
|---|---|---|
| `bw` | bigWig | coverage (ATAC-seq, RNA-seq) |
| `quantdir` | a Salmon output folder (with `quant.sf`) | `transcript_counts` |
| `paired-end` | BEDPE or BED12 | splice junctions |
| `hic` | `.hic`, `.cool`, `.mcool` | Hi-C contact map |
| `bed` | BED12 | annotation |

If you would rather not write it by hand, or already have a sample sheet with the same
information, paste this section and your file list (or sheet) into an AI assistant and ask it
for a `samples.txt`.

Then open it like the example: `run_plottrellis(project_dir = "my-project", samples_txt =
"path/to/samples.txt")`. Editing the `samples.txt` later updates the project the next time
it is opened.

# More in code

- **Tracks** are listed top to bottom. `pt_tracks(proj)` lists every one the project has.
  `genes`, `transcripts_annotated` and the other annotation tracks need no sample; the rest
  name theirs after `@`.
- **Comparisons** name two samples, the second being the reference:
  `"junctions_diff@KO vs Control"`.
- **`parallel = TRUE`** repeats every track written without `@` for each sample, so
  `pt_figure(proj, "Elf5", c("atac", "transcript_counts", "transcripts_annotated", "genes"),
  parallel = TRUE)` is the
  figure above. `parallel = c("LP", "Basal")` picks the samples and their order.
- **`region = "chr2:103,400,000-103,460,000"`** instead of a gene shows any coordinates.
- **`pt_script(fig, "Elf5.R")`** writes a standalone script that redraws the figure, for
  edits the API doesn't offer.
- **`run_plottrellis(proj)`** opens the same project in the app, and
  `pt_preload(proj, fig)` makes it open on `fig`, ready for someone who doesn't code.

Everything a project keeps (settings, a copy of its samples table, caches) is in its
`project_dir`; your data files stay where they are.

# Sharing

To pass your data to someone else, send them the path to your `samples.txt` (for a wizard
project, the `project_samples.txt` in its folder). They run the same command with a
`project_dir` of their own:

```{r sharing, eval=FALSE}
run_plottrellis(project_dir = "tcell-project",
                samples_txt = "/data/smithlab/tcell_2026/samples.txt")
```

They need to be able to read your data files, so keep them on a shared drive and give
`data_root` and `gtf_path` as full paths. To have the app open on a gene with its tracks
already picked, as the example does, add two header lines:

```
# start_gene: Elf5
# start_tracks: atac@Basal, atac@LP, transcripts_annotated, genes
```
